unit.title: The 2026 reset
unit.summary: The new cars: active aero, the 50/50 power unit, Overtake Mode and the new teams.

lessons.title: Why F1 reset the rules
lessons.objective: Explain what a regulation era is and what 2026 was meant to change.

payload.prompt: What is a regulation era in F1?

options.text: A multi-year rulebook cycle; a new one means big redesigns and a reshuffled pecking order.
options.explanation: Right. A new era means new rules for everyone, so teams redesign their cars and the order can shake up.

options.text: A single season where the rules change slightly.
options.explanation: No, regulation eras last multiple years. Rule tweaks happen within an era.

options.text: A penalty for breaking the FIA regulations.
options.explanation: That is a grid penalty or points deduction, not a regulation era.

options.text: A requirement to change engines every other year.
options.explanation: Engine supply is set within an era, but a regulation era is about the whole rulebook.

explanation.correct: Right. A regulation era lasts several years with a broadly fixed rulebook. When a new one starts, the cars and power units are redesigned and the pecking order can reshuffle.
explanation.incorrect: A regulation era is a multi-year rulebook cycle. 2026 begins a new one, so car design and performance hierarchies reset.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2026 begins a new regulation era.

payload.prompt: Why did F1 reset the rules for 2026?

options.text: To make lighter, nimbler cars with more electric power and sustainable fuel, and to attract new manufacturers.
options.explanation: Right. 2026 was designed around greener technology, better racing and bringing in new engine makers.

options.text: Because Mercedes and Red Bull were too fast.
options.explanation: A new rulebook does reset the order, but that was not the stated goal. The goals were sustainability, better racing and new entrants.

options.text: To make the races shorter.
options.explanation: Race distance is unchanged. The reset is about car design and power units.

options.text: To reduce the cost cap.
options.explanation: The cost cap has applied since 2021 and is a separate rule. The 2026 reset is about the cars and power units.

explanation.correct: Right. 2026 brought active aero, a 50/50 power split, sustainable fuel, smaller lighter cars, and new teams like Audi and Cadillac.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 reset brought Audi and Red Bull-Ford in as engine makers and welcomed Honda back. It was built around sustainability and a 50/50 power unit.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2026 reset to bring in new manufacturers and greener technology.

payload.prompt: Match each 2026 goal to what it means.

pairs.definition: A multi-year rulebook cycle; 2026 begins a new one with fresh car designs and reset power hierarchies.
A yearly limit on team spending (about $215 million, with exceptions) that has applied since 2021.
100% advanced fuel made from non-food biomass, waste or captured carbon, not fossil fuels.

distractorDefinitions: A penalty for breaking F1's environmental rules.
A system that recycles old tyres into fuel.

explanation.summary: The 2026 reset is a new rulebook with greener fuel, running alongside the cost cap that has applied since 2021.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2026 is a fresh rulebook with greener fuel.

statement.speaker: Your friend
statement.text: Why do they keep changing the rules? The cars look totally different this year.

payload.question: What is a good way to explain it?

options.text: The rules are planned in multi-year cycles, and 2026 is the start of a new one.
options.explanation: Yes. A regulation era is planned years ahead, which is why the cars look so different in a year when a new one starts.

options.text: They rewrite the rulebook before every race.
options.explanation: Rules are tweaked during a season, but big overhauls come in planned multi-year cycles, not race by race.

options.text: They change the rules so a particular team loses.
options.explanation: A new era does reshuffle the order, but the changes are planned around bigger goals, not aimed at one team.

payload.translation: F1 works in regulation eras, long rulebook cycles. A new era means redesigned cars and power units, so a big change this year is normal.

followUps.line: Do you think the new cars are better to watch?
followUps.why: Invites her opinion instead of pretending you know, and keeps the chat going.

followUps.line: Which change do you notice most?
followUps.why: Lets her show what she likes about the new rules, which is a great way to learn.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need every detail of the new rules. Knowing that eras are planned multi-year resets is enough, then ask what she makes of them.

lessons.title: Smaller, lighter, narrower cars
lessons.objective: Describe how the 2026 cars differ in size, weight and downforce.

payload.prompt: Guess: what is the minimum weight of a 2026 F1 car and driver, in kilograms?

explanation.correct: Right. The 2026 cars are lighter at 768 kg minimum, down about 30 kg from the 2022 to 2025 era. Smaller, narrower and lighter.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 minimum weight is 768 kilograms, about 30 kilograms lighter than the previous era. That is a deliberate reset.
explanation.sayThisLine: The minimum weight dropped for 2026.

payload.prompt: Why are the 2026 cars smaller and lighter?

options.text: To make them more nimble and efficient, with less weight and drag, so they can follow each other more closely.
options.explanation: Right. A smaller, lighter car with less drag is more agile and efficient, and it makes less disturbed air for the car behind.

options.text: To make the cars faster and more spectacular.
options.explanation: The aim was not simply more speed. Less weight and less downforce mean the cars are designed to race closer and use energy better.

options.text: Because narrower tyres are cheaper.
options.explanation: Cost was not the reason. The car got smaller and lighter as part of the new performance and efficiency goals.

options.text: To make it easier for new teams to enter.
options.explanation: Attracting new entrants was a goal of the 2026 package, but shrinking the car was about agility, efficiency and closer racing.

explanation.correct: Right. The 2022 to 2025 cars were big and heavy. The 2026 cars are smaller, lighter and less draggy by design, so they are nimbler and can follow one another more easily.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 cars are smaller and lighter, with less downforce and drag than the 2022 to 2025 cars. The aim is agility, efficiency and closer racing.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2026 cars are smaller and lighter by design.

payload.prompt: What is ground effect, and how does it change for 2026?

options.text: Air under the floor is shaped to create suction, pushing the car down. 2026 cars get less of their grip from it.
options.explanation: Right. The 2022 to 2025 cars made a lot of downforce from the floor; the 2026 rules dial that back and leave the wings to do more.

options.text: Ground effect is when the track is bumpy and affects handling. 2026 tracks are smoother.
options.explanation: No, ground effect is aerodynamic. It is the shaped floor that creates downforce by speeding air underneath.

options.text: It is the effect of low fuel loads on lap time. 2026 allows more fuel.
options.explanation: That is not ground effect. Ground effect is how the underfloor creates downforce.

options.text: It is a safety system that stops the car if it gets too low. 2026 removed it.
options.explanation: That is not ground effect. The shaped floor creating suction is ground effect.

explanation.correct: Right. Ground effect is the shaped floor speeding air underneath, which creates low pressure that sucks the car down. The 2026 cars make less downforce this way.
explanation.incorrect: Ground effect is aerodynamic suction from the underfloor, not bumps or a safety system. The 2022 to 2025 cars relied on it heavily; the 2026 cars rely on it less.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ground effect is the floor sucking the car down, and the new cars have less of it.

payload.prompt: Do the 2026 cars have less downforce than the 2022-2025 cars?

scene.alt: A 2026 F1 car with active aero wings.

explanation.correct: Right. The 2026 cars make less downforce, and less drag too, than the 2022 to 2025 cars. That is part of making them lighter, more efficient and easier to follow.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. The 2026 cars are designed with less downforce and less drag than the 2022 to 2025 cars. Active aero then lets each car trade between the two during a lap.

payload.prompt: Are the 2026 cars' floor and tyres narrower than in 2022-2025?

scene.alt: Text only: a comparison of car width, with the newer car slimmer in the floor and tyres.

explanation.correct: Right. Both the floor and the tyres are narrower in 2026. It is part of making the car smaller and lighter, and it cuts ground-effect suction and drag.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, the 2026 cars have a narrower floor and narrower tyres. Along with a shorter wheelbase and lower weight, it is one of the ways the cars were made smaller.

lessons.title: The 50/50 power unit
lessons.objective: Explain what the power unit is made of now and what disappeared.

payload.prompt: Match each part of the 2026 power unit to what it does.

pairs.definition: The 1.6-litre turbocharged V6, producing roughly 400 kW in 2026.
The electric motor-generator on the drivetrain: recovers braking energy and adds up to 350 kW.
The high-voltage battery holding harvested energy for deployment during a lap.

distractorDefinitions: A heat-recovery system on the turbo charger.
A fuel tank that stores sustainable fuel.

explanation.summary: The 2026 power unit is roughly 50/50: combustion engine and MGU-K electrical system sharing the work.
explanation.sayThisLine: It is the engine plus the battery, about half and half.

payload.prompt: What did the MGU-H do, and why is it gone in 2026?

pairs.definition: The motor-generator on the turbo that recovered energy from exhaust heat. Deleted for 2026.
It was costly and complex, and dropping it made the unit simpler to build and easier for newcomers to join.
The MGU-K on the drivetrain now does all the electrical recovery, and it was made more powerful.

distractorDefinitions: The MGU-H was unreliable and teams wanted it gone.
It was removed to reduce fuel consumption.

explanation.summary: The MGU-H was complex and costly. Removing it simplifies the power unit, and a little turbo lag is one result, so drivers have more to manage.
explanation.sayThisLine: The MGU-H is gone, so the power units are simpler and there is a bit more turbo lag.

payload.prompt: Where is the MGU-K on a 2026 F1 car, relative to the engine?

diagram.alt: Side view of a Formula 1 car showing the cockpit, halo, engine and rear suspension.

explanation.correct: Right. The MGU-K is on the drivetrain, recovering energy from braking through the wheels.
explanation.incorrect: The MGU-K sits on the gearbox or drivetrain, where it can harvest braking energy from the wheels and add power to the drivetrain.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about the energy store.
payload.template: The energy store is a high-voltage {{what}} that holds energy recovered under braking for use on the {{where}}.

explanation.correct: Right. The energy store is the car's battery. The MGU-K fills it under braking, and the car deploys that energy for extra power, mostly on the straights.
explanation.incorrect: The energy store is the hybrid battery, not a fuel tank. It is topped up when the car brakes and spent for extra power when the driver accelerates, mostly on the straights.

payload.prompt: What does '50/50 power unit' mean in 2026?

options.text: The combustion engine and the electric side (MGU-K) each supply roughly half the peak power, about 400 kW and up to 350 kW.
options.explanation: Right. At peak, the V6 gives around 400 kW and the electric motor up to 350 kW, so the split is close to even.

options.text: Half the cars run on electricity and half on fuel.
options.explanation: No, every car is a hybrid: a combustion engine plus an electric system. The split is inside each car, not across the grid.

options.text: The engine and gearbox share equal power.
options.explanation: The gearbox transfers power; the 50/50 is about combustion versus electrical energy.

options.text: The 2026 cars are half as powerful as the 2025 cars.
options.explanation: No, the total power is similar to before. The change is where it comes from: far more of it is now electric.

explanation.correct: Right. 2026 is designed so the combustion engine and the electrical system (battery and MGU-K) share the power output roughly equally.
explanation.incorrect: The 50/50 split means the V6 and the electrical system (recovery and deployment) contribute similar power. It is a deliberate balance.
explanation.sayThisLine: It is roughly half from the engine, half from the battery.

lessons.title: Straight Mode and Corner Mode
lessons.objective: Explain how active aero works and how it differs from DRS.

payload.prompt: What is active aero?

options.text: Front and rear wing elements that move during a lap, switching between a high-downforce mode and a low-drag mode.
options.explanation: Right. The wings change shape on the move: low drag for the straights, high downforce for braking and corners.

options.text: A rear wing that only opens when a chasing car is close.
options.explanation: That describes DRS, which is gone. Active aero moves front and rear wing elements on every car.

options.text: Flexible wings that bend under load to reduce drag.
options.explanation: That is a flexi-wing, which is about a wing bending under load. Active aero is deliberate, controlled movement.

options.text: The same as DRS, just renamed for 2026.
options.explanation: No. DRS was a single rear flap that only a chasing car could open. Active aero moves both wings and is used by every car.

explanation.correct: Right. Active aero is new for 2026: front and rear wing elements that move, so a car can run low drag on the straights and high downforce in the corners.
explanation.incorrect: Active aero means moveable wing elements on the front and rear wings that change during a lap. Unlike DRS, which is gone, it is for every car and is not tied to a rival's gap.
explanation.sayThisLine: Active aero lets the wings open for speed on the straights.

payload.prompt: What is Straight Mode (also called X-mode)?

options.text: A low-drag wing setting for the straights: the wings flatten to cut drag and add top speed.
options.explanation: Right. Straight Mode is the low-drag set-up: less downforce, less drag, more speed on the straight.

options.text: A high-downforce setting that helps the car corner faster.
options.explanation: That is Corner Mode. Straight Mode is the opposite, trading grip for speed.

options.text: A mode where the car drives in a straight line automatically.
options.explanation: No, Straight Mode is just the wing position. The driver still drives.

options.text: A penalty box where cars are sent for rule breaks.
options.explanation: That is not related to modes. Straight Mode is an aero setting.

explanation.correct: Right. In Straight Mode the wings flatten for minimal drag. Fans call it X-mode, and it is used to gain speed on the straights.
explanation.incorrect: Straight Mode (X-mode) is the low-downforce, low-drag wing setting for straights. It is a wing position, not a penalty or an autopilot.
explanation.sayThisLine: Straight mode on the back straight and boom, he is gone.

payload.prompt: Does Corner Mode (Z-mode) give more downforce than Straight Mode?

scene.alt: A 2026 F1 car with wings in high-downforce position before a corner.

explanation.correct: Right. Corner Mode (Z-mode) is the high-downforce setting: the wings move to generate grip for braking and turning.
explanation.incorrect: Yes. Corner Mode is the high-downforce setting, the opposite of Straight Mode, used for corners and braking zones.

payload.prompt: Does a car need to be within a second of a rival to use Straight Mode?

scene.alt: Text only: a car running with its wings open on a straight, with no other car nearby.

choices.label: No, any car can use it

explanation.correct: Right. Straight Mode is an aero setting for every car, whether it is leading or chasing. The one-second rule belongs to Overtake Mode, which is a separate electrical boost.
explanation.incorrect: Straight Mode is not tied to a gap. Any car can run its wings in low-drag mode where the rules allow. The within-one-second rule applies to Overtake Mode instead.

lessons.title: Overtake Mode and Boost
lessons.objective: Explain who gets Overtake Mode and how Boost differs.

payload.prompt: Who can use Overtake Mode in 2026?

options.text: A driver within one second of the car directly ahead at a detection point on the track.
options.explanation: Right. Overtake Mode is for the chaser: a driver within one second of the car ahead at the detection point gets extra electrical deployment.

options.text: Only the car ahead, to defend.
options.explanation: No, it is for the follower. The car ahead cannot activate Overtake Mode.

options.text: Any driver at any time.
options.explanation: No, you must be within one second of the car ahead to qualify.

options.text: Only at circuits with long straights, like Monza.
options.explanation: Overtake Mode is about the gap to the car ahead, not the track layout. It applies at every circuit.

explanation.correct: Right. Overtake Mode goes to a car within one second of the car ahead at the detection point. It took over from DRS as the chaser's help.
explanation.incorrect: Overtake Mode is for a driver trailing by one second or less at the detection point. It replaced DRS as the chaser's help for 2026.
explanation.sayThisLine: Within one second, you get Overtake Mode.

payload.prompt: What is the Boost button?

options.text: A manual driver button for extra electrical deployment, limited in how much and how often it can be used.
options.explanation: Right. The driver presses it to deploy more battery power for a burst of speed, but it is rationed, so it cannot be used all the time.

options.text: An automatic system that gives extra power to any car that is falling behind.
options.explanation: No, Boost is a button the driver presses, and it is limited. It is not an automatic help for slower cars.

options.text: The same as Overtake Mode, just a different name.
options.explanation: They are different. Overtake Mode depends on being within one second of the car ahead; Boost is a driver's button.

options.text: A penalty that adds speed to a car that has broken a rule.
options.explanation: Boost is a tool, not a penalty. It gives the driver more control over energy deployment.

explanation.correct: Right. Boost is a driver-activated button to deploy extra battery power. It is limited, so drivers and teams must choose when it is worth spending.
explanation.incorrect: Boost is a manual electrical deployment tool: the driver presses a button for extra speed, but there are limits on how much and how often it can be used.
explanation.sayThisLine: He hit the boost button on the last lap.

payload.prompt: Is Overtake Mode a wing setting, like Straight Mode?

scene.alt: Text only: two labels side by side, one for a wing setting and one for an electrical power boost.

choices.label: No, it is extra electrical power

explanation.correct: Right. Straight Mode and Corner Mode are wing settings. Overtake Mode is extra electrical deployment for a car that has closed to within a second of the one ahead.
explanation.incorrect: Overtake Mode is about power, not wings. It gives a close chaser extra electrical deployment, while Straight and Corner Modes change the wing position.

payload.prompt: Can a driver use the Boost button as many times as they want during a race?

scene.alt: A driver reaching for the boost button on the steering wheel.

explanation.correct: Right. Boost is rationed: there are limits on how much and how often it can be used, so drivers must spend it wisely.
explanation.incorrect: No, Boost is limited. Because there are caps on how much and how often it can be used, choosing when to press it matters.

payload.prompt: Use Overtake Mode and Boost for this pass now, or hold them back?

situation.narrative: You are 0.9 seconds behind the car ahead, inside the window for Overtake Mode. A long straight, the best passing spot on the lap, is coming up.

facts.label: Race stage
facts.value: Mid-race, plenty of laps to go

options.label: Use both now and go for the pass
options.consequence: You close up on the straight with extra electrical power, have a good chance to pass, and gain track position while the passing spot is right in front of you.
considerations: The gap is inside a second and the best passing spot is here.
Track position is worth a lot, and there is still some Boost left for later.

options.label: Hold back and save Boost for later
options.consequence: You keep more energy in reserve, but you may not get another chance this good, and the car ahead may pull clear or pit first.
considerations: Saving energy makes sense if the pass is unlikely to work.
Here the chance is good, so waiting risks losing it.

payload.expertNote: Energy is a budget, like tyres. Spending it where it wins a place is usually better than saving it for a moment that may never come, as long as you keep enough in reserve to defend.
payload.sayThisLine: He had the gap and the straight, so he went for it.

lessons.title: Recharging: where the energy comes from
lessons.objective: Say where a car harvests energy and what it costs.

payload.prompt: Where does a 2026 car harvest energy during a lap?

options.text: Mainly under braking, using the MGU-K on the drivetrain, and from engine power when cruising.
options.explanation: Right. Braking is the big source: as the car slows, the MGU-K captures energy. The engine can also charge the battery, and lifting off adds a little more.

options.text: Only on straights by coasting.
options.explanation: Coasting helps, but braking is the main harvest point. Coasting on its own is not the main source.

options.text: From the turbo's waste heat, like the MGU-H did.
options.explanation: The MGU-H is gone in 2026. Harvesting is through the drivetrain (MGU-K) now.

options.text: Automatically without any cost to the driver.
options.explanation: Braking recovers energy, but aggressive harvesting through lift-and-coast costs lap time.

explanation.correct: Right. Braking under the MGU-K is the main harvest. The driver can also lift off and coast to recharge the battery, which costs speed.
explanation.incorrect: The MGU-K on the drivetrain harvests braking energy. Additionally, drivers can lift and coast to top up the battery, trading speed for energy.
explanation.sayThisLine: Braking is where you harvest energy.

payload.prompt: Match each energy strategy to what it means.

pairs.definition: Refilling the battery from braking and engine power, done constantly during every lap.
When the battery runs out on a straight, the car stops getting electrical help and even slows as it forces a recharge.
Easing off the throttle early before braking to let the battery recharge and save fuel.

distractorDefinitions: Coasting down from a mountain without power.

explanation.summary: Energy management is the race: teams harvest on brakes, deploy on straights, and lift to recharge. Clipping is the price of an empty battery.
explanation.sayThisLine: Recharge under braking, deploy on the straight, clip if you run out.

payload.prompt: A driver lifts off early to recharge the battery. Does that cost him lap time?

scene.alt: Text only: a driver lifts off the throttle well before the braking point to bank energy for the next straight.

choices.label: No, it is a free recharge

explanation.correct: Right. Lifting off early means arriving at the braking point slower, which costs a little lap time. The driver is trading a bit of time now for energy to deploy later.
explanation.incorrect: It is not free. Easing off before the braking point loses a little time each lap, so teams only ask for it when the energy or fuel saved is worth more than the time lost.

payload.prompt: The battery is already full. Can the car still store energy from braking?

scene.alt: Text only: a car braking for a corner while its battery gauge already reads full.

choices.label: No, there is nowhere to put it

explanation.correct: Right. A full battery cannot take more charge. The car still brakes, but the extra energy is lost as heat instead of being saved, which is why teams plan when to spend and when to recharge.
explanation.incorrect: A battery can only hold so much. Once it is full, braking energy cannot be stored, so it is wasted as heat. That is why energy has to be spent on the straights to make room.

lessons.title: Sustainable fuel
lessons.objective: Explain what sustainable fuel is and what it changes for fans.

payload.prompt: What is sustainable fuel in 2026 F1?

options.text: 100% advanced fuel made from non-food biomass, waste or captured carbon, not fossil fuel.
options.explanation: Right. The carbon it releases was taken from the air or from waste, so its net carbon footprint is far lower than fossil fuel's.

options.text: Electric fuel that does not burn.
options.explanation: F1 2026 still uses a combustion engine. The fuel is different, but it still burns.

options.text: Fuel mixed with 50% electricity.
options.explanation: No. The electricity comes from the battery and MGU-K separately. Sustainable fuel is a liquid fuel for the combustion engine.

options.text: Cheaper fuel to reduce team costs.
options.explanation: It is not about saving money. Sustainable fuel is about environmental impact.

explanation.correct: Right. For 2026 the fuel is fully sustainable: a drop-in replacement for fossil fuel made from sources like non-food biomass, waste or captured carbon.
explanation.incorrect: Sustainable fuel is a liquid fuel that burns in a normal combustion engine, made from advanced biomass, waste or captured carbon instead of fossil sources.
explanation.sayThisLine: The fuel is 100% sustainable now, not fossil fuel.

payload.prompt: Was sustainable fuel brought in to cut the engine's power?

scene.alt: Text only: a question about why the 2026 rules introduced fully sustainable fuel.

explanation.correct: Right. The aim was to cut net carbon emissions and show that top-level racing can run on a sustainable fuel, while still pushing fuel makers to innovate. It was not about slowing the cars.
explanation.incorrect: Sustainable fuel is about environmental impact, not reducing power. The engine still has to make around 400 kW; it just burns a fuel with a much lower net carbon footprint.
explanation.sayThisLine: They went sustainable to cut emissions, not to slow the cars.

payload.prompt: Complete the sentence about the 2026 fuel.
payload.template: The 2026 fuel is {{fuel-type}}, made from biomass, waste or captured carbon instead of crude oil.

explanation.correct: Right. Sustainable fuel is made from sources like non-food biomass, waste or captured carbon, and it works as a drop-in replacement for fossil fuel.
explanation.incorrect: Fossil fuel comes from crude oil, and an electric fuel would not burn in a combustion engine. The 2026 fuel is a sustainable liquid fuel.

payload.prompt: Say what the fuel change means for the 2026 cars.
payload.template: The 2026 cars still burn fuel in a {{engine}}, but the fuel has a {{impact}} net carbon impact.

explanation.correct: Right. The 2026 cars still have a turbocharged V6 that burns fuel, with an electric motor alongside. The fuel is what changed: it has a far lower net carbon impact.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 cars are hybrids with a turbo V6 and an electric motor, not a V10 or electric-only. The change is the fuel, which has a much lower net carbon impact than fossil fuel.

lessons.title: Audi, Cadillac, Ford, Honda: who is new
lessons.objective: Identify the new teams and engine partnerships.

payload.prompt: Match each new entrant to their role in 2026.

pairs.definition: A works team on the former Sauber entry, building its own power unit and racing as Audi.
The 11th team for 2026, on Ferrari power for now, with a General Motors engine planned.
A manufacturer partnered with Red Bull's own power-unit programme, which supplies Red Bull and Racing Bulls.

distractorDefinitions: An engine that runs on liquid hydrogen.
A team that makes parts for other constructors.

explanation.summary: Audi is a works team, Cadillac is the 11th team, and Ford partners Red Bull's power units. The 2026 grid grew and gained new engine names.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2026 brought new teams and new engine makers.

payload.prompt: Match each engine supplier to the teams using it.

pairs.definition: Supplies power units to Haas and Cadillac, plus its own works team.
Supplies power units to McLaren, Williams and Alpine, plus its own works team.
Back in F1 as Aston Martin's works-style power unit partner for 2026.

distractorDefinitions: Supplies engines to exactly one team per manufacturer.
Does not sell engines to customer teams.

explanation.summary: The 2026 power unit makers are Ferrari, Mercedes, Honda, Audi and Red Bull-Ford. Ferrari and Mercedes supply several teams, while Audi supplies only itself.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ferrari, Mercedes, Honda, Audi and Red Bull-Ford power the 2026 grid.

payload.prompt: What makes Audi special as a new team in 2026?

options.text: Audi is a works team that builds its own power unit, rather than buying one.
options.explanation: Right. Audi is a manufacturer entering with a works team, taking over the Sauber entry and building its own power unit.

options.text: Audi buys engines from Ferrari.
options.explanation: No, Audi makes its own power unit. That is what makes it a works team.

options.text: Audi is a junior team run by Red Bull.
options.explanation: No. Red Bull's sister team is Racing Bulls. Audi is its own manufacturer team.

options.text: Audi races with a Mercedes power unit.
options.explanation: No. Mercedes supplies McLaren, Williams and Alpine. Audi builds its own power unit.

explanation.correct: Right. Audi builds its own power unit and runs its own team, which is what makes it a works team rather than a customer.
explanation.incorrect: Audi is a works team and power unit manufacturer for 2026, on the former Sauber entry. It builds its own power unit instead of buying one.
explanation.sayThisLine: Audi is a new works team and power unit maker.

payload.prompt: Why is Cadillac an 11th team for 2026 instead of 10?

options.text: An eleventh entry, backed by General Motors, was approved to join the existing ten teams.
options.explanation: Right. Cadillac is an addition to the grid, backed by General Motors, rather than a replacement for anyone.

options.text: Because one of the existing teams left F1.
options.explanation: No, all other teams stayed. Cadillac is an addition, not a replacement.

options.text: To match the number of constructors to the number of engine makers.
options.explanation: That is not why. Cadillac's entry was independent of the engine supplier count.

options.text: Cadillac is just a temporary partner team.
options.explanation: Cadillac is a full entry competing for both titles, not a temporary guest.

explanation.correct: Right. Cadillac's entry for 2026 was added on top of the existing ten teams, which is why the grid now has eleven teams and 22 cars.
explanation.incorrect: Cadillac was approved as an additional entry, so the grid grew from ten teams to eleven. It competes for both the drivers' and constructors' championships.
explanation.sayThisLine: Cadillac is the eleventh team, a brand-new entry for 2026.

payload.prompt: Which of these are new engine suppliers entering F1 for 2026?

diagram.alt: Logos representing F1 engine makers and manufacturers.

explanation.correct: Right. Audi, Honda and Red Bull-Ford are new. Mercedes, Ferrari and Alpine continue from before.
explanation.incorrect: Audi (works team), Honda (Aston Martin) and Red Bull-Ford are new. Mercedes and Ferrari already supplied engines; Alpine switched from Renault power to Mercedes.

payload.prompt: In 2026, F1 has {{num}} engine suppliers: Ferrari, Mercedes, Honda, Audi and {{new-one}}.
payload.template: In 2026, F1 has {{num}} engine suppliers: Ferrari, Mercedes, Honda, Audi and {{new-one}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Five engine suppliers in 2026: the big three (Ferrari, Mercedes) plus three new makers (Honda, Audi, Red Bull-Ford).
explanation.incorrect: Five suppliers for 2026: Ferrari, Mercedes, Honda, Audi and Red Bull-Ford. Alpine switched to Mercedes power for 2026.
